modules.title: The water we swim in
modules.goal: Recognize that Minnesota's majority culture is a culture, and understand why it is hard to see from inside.
modules.body:
## Opening

Here is some humor, written by Minnesotans about Minnesotans. In 1987 Howard Mohr, a writer for *A Prairie Home Companion*, published *How to Talk Minnesotan: A Visitor's Guide* ([MPR News, Sept. 6, 2022](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2022/09/06/author-howard-mohr-known-for-how-to-talk-minnesotan-dies)). It taught visitors that "That's different" is "a blanket reply on neutral ground." It explained that a guest must refuse food and the host must insist. And it described the "Minnesota Long Goodbye," which ends with the guests in the car and the hosts bent at the driver's window ([Duluth News Tribune via Echo Press, Sept. 6, 2022](https://www.echopress.com/lifestyle/arts-and-entertainment/front-row-seat-remembering-howard-mohr-and-how-to-talk-minnesotan)).

If you smiled, you probably recognized something. That is the point. Habits like these feel like plain good manners to the people who grew up with them. To someone from elsewhere, they can look like a set of rules nobody wrote down. This module is about that gap: what it means that the way "we" do things is a culture, too.

## What the fish cannot see

In a 2005 commencement speech, the novelist David Foster Wallace told a short parable. Two young fish meet an older fish, who asks them how the water is. Later, one young fish turns to the other and asks, "What the hell is water?" Wallace's point was that the most obvious and important realities are often the hardest to see and talk about ([Farnam Street transcript of Wallace's Kenyon speech](https://fs.blog/david-foster-wallace-this-is-water/)).

Most training on culture asks staff to learn about other people's cultures. That matters. But the culture a person grew up in rarely feels like a culture at all. It feels like "normal," the neutral background against which everyone else looks "cultural." For many people in Minnesota's public agencies, mainstream Minnesota culture is the water.

:::voice
Milton Bennett writes that people often experience their own culture as more "central to reality" than others ([Bennett, 2017](https://www.idrinstitute.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/DMIS-IDRI.pdf)).
:::

Bennett, an intercultural researcher, adds a second point that is easy to miss. The categories people have for seeing their own culture are far more detailed than the ones they have for anyone else's ([Bennett, Developmental Model of Intercultural Sensitivity, IDRI, 2017](https://www.idrinstitute.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/DMIS-IDRI.pdf)). If you grew up here, you may be able to tell many kinds of Minnesota "no" apart. You may have far fewer ways to read a "no" from a family whose culture differs from yours.

Put plainly, the people least likely to notice how culture shapes a meeting, a form or a service plan are often the people whose culture shaped them. That is not a flaw in anyone. It is how being inside a culture works.

Seeing your own culture is not the same as criticizing it. Minnesota's majority culture has real gifts, from its cooperatives and civic habits to its volunteering and its early civil rights laws. Later modules look at those strengths with respect. It has also, by the testimony of many Minnesotans of color, immigrants and newcomers, made some things hard to say out loud. Both can be true at once.

Three cautions apply throughout this course:

- **Patterns are not people.** A pattern found across a state or a country describes an average. It cannot tell you how a particular coworker, family or client thinks.
- **"Minnesota culture" is plural.** The majority culture grew mostly from Northern European, Protestant and Catholic, farm and small-town roots. Minnesotans of every background now share in it and change it, and many live in more than one culture at once.
- **Evidence varies in strength.** Some points rest on large surveys. Others rest on interviews, essays or humor. The course tells you which is which.

Even the humor in the opening comes with a caution. Writing after Mohr's death, Jay Gabler noted that the book described how one strain of Minnesotans talked, not all Minnesotans ([Duluth News Tribune via Echo Press, Sept. 6, 2022](https://www.echopress.com/lifestyle/arts-and-entertainment/front-row-seat-remembering-howard-mohr-and-how-to-talk-minnesotan)).

:::voice
Gabler called it "a certain, then culturally dominant, strain" of Minnesotans ([Echo Press, 2022](https://www.echopress.com/lifestyle/arts-and-entertainment/front-row-seat-remembering-howard-mohr-and-how-to-talk-minnesotan)).
:::

## Who Minnesotans are now

If the majority culture is the water, it helps to know who is swimming in it. The numbers show a majority that is still large, and a state that is changing fast.

**The majority, counted more than one way.** The Census Bureau's 2024 American Community Survey counts 5,793,151 Minnesotans. Of those, 4,329,205, or 74.7 percent, identified as white alone and not Hispanic ([Census Bureau, ACS 2024, table B03002, via Census Reporter](https://api.censusreporter.org/1.0/data/show/latest?table_ids=B03002&geo_ids=04000US27)). Counting everyone who marked white as their only race, Hispanic or not, the share is 75.9 percent. Counting everyone who marked white alone or with another race, it is 82.8 percent ([ACS 2024, tables B02001 and B02008](https://api.censusreporter.org/1.0/data/show/latest?table_ids=B02001,B02008,B05012,B05002&geo_ids=04000US27)). The definition changes the number, so it is worth naming which one you use.

Minnesota Compass reports about 74 percent of Minnesotans as non-Hispanic white, down from 83 percent in 2010, and about 1.5 million Minnesotans of color, or 26 percent ([Minnesota Compass, by race and ethnicity](https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/race-ethnicity)).

**The young are far more diverse than the old.** This may be the single most important fact for a public agency.

:::fact
People of color are 7 percent of Minnesotans 80 and older, but 42 percent of children under 5 ([Minnesota Compass](https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/race-ethnicity)).
:::

The people who lead and staff institutions tend to be older than the people those institutions will serve in twenty years.

**Immigrants, then and now.** About 9 percent of Minnesotans were born abroad in 2024, up from 5 percent in 2000. That is far below the 37 percent of the late 1800s. One in five Minnesota children is the child of an immigrant, and Mexican and Somali immigrants are the two largest immigrant groups ([Minnesota Compass, by immigrant group](https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/immigration)). In other words, today's majority culture was itself built by immigrants, at a time when the share of newcomers was about four times what it is now.

**Homegrown.** Of everyone living in Minnesota in 2024, about 66 percent were born here ([ACS 2024, table B05002](https://api.censusreporter.org/1.0/data/show/latest?table_ids=B02001,B02008,B05012,B05002&geo_ids=04000US27)). In 2012 MPR News reported that about seven in ten Minnesotans were born in the state, against roughly six in ten nationally ([MPR News, March 12, 2012](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2012/03/12/outsiders1-is-minnesota-nice-to-newcomers)). A large homegrown majority is one reason local ways of doing things can feel settled, and hard for newcomers to enter. Module 2 returns to that.

**Metro and Greater Minnesota.** About 55 percent of Minnesotans live in the Twin Cities region and about 45 percent in Greater Minnesota ([Minnesota Compass, all Minnesotans, 2020 to 2024](https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/cultural-communities/minnesota)). The majority culture shows up in both places, with different accents.

## Who works in state government

Now turn the lens on ourselves. Minnesota Management and Budget's workforce report for fiscal year 2023 (July 2022 to June 2023) counts about 37,100 executive branch positions across 87 agencies, boards and commissions. DHS is the largest agency, with about one in five executive branch employees ([MMB, State of Minnesota Workforce Planning Report FY 2023](https://www.lrl.mn.gov/docs/2024/other/240792.pdf)).

- **Race and ethnicity.** About 15.9 percent of executive branch employees identified as Black, Indigenous or People of Color (BIPOC), 78.5 percent as white, and about 5 percent did not report race. That compares with 20.4 percent BIPOC in the Minnesota labor force. Hispanic and Latino workers are the most underrepresented, at 2.9 percent of state workers against 5.4 percent of the labor force. BIPOC employees were 21 percent of new hires in FY 2023, up from 11 percent in FY 2011 ([MMB FY 2023](https://www.lrl.mn.gov/docs/2024/other/240792.pdf)).
- **Disability.** Employees with disabilities were 11.6 percent of the executive branch, about twice their 5.9 percent share of the state labor force in the report's comparison ([MMB FY 2023](https://www.lrl.mn.gov/docs/2024/other/240792.pdf)).
- **Age.** The median age of state workers was 46, and about 40 percent were 50 or older. The median age of new hires was 36 ([MMB FY 2023](https://www.lrl.mn.gov/docs/2024/other/240792.pdf)).

:::fact
The report lists 7,360 DHS employees: 20.0 percent people of color, 78.1 percent white, and 12.1 percent reporting a disability ([MMB FY 2023, appendix table](https://www.lrl.mn.gov/docs/2024/other/240792.pdf)).
:::

So DHS is somewhat more racially diverse than the executive branch as a whole, and close to the state's labor force. The report does not compare DHS staff with the people DHS serves. Set beside Compass's finding about the youngest Minnesotans, though, the age gap between state staff and the state's future population is clear.

What these numbers do not show matters just as much. The workforce report covers race, sex, disability, veteran status and age ([MMB FY 2023](https://www.lrl.mn.gov/docs/2024/other/240792.pdf)). No published source was found that says where state or DHS employees grew up, how many were born in Minnesota, what languages they speak, or what religious or cultural backgrounds they come from. Race is not the same as culture. A white employee may have grown up in a recent immigrant family. An employee of color may have grown up entirely inside Minnesota's majority culture. The numbers describe who is in the room, not how anyone in it thinks.

## A mirror, not a label

So why start a course here? Because the habits of a majority culture tend to become the default settings of its institutions. In a public agency, those settings show up in how meetings run, how feedback is given, how forms are worded, and what counts as a "good" plan. When most of the people setting the defaults share one culture, the defaults can feel neutral. They are not neutral. They are simply familiar to some people and not to others.

This course uses a few frameworks from researchers, starting with Bennett's. Each one is offered as a mirror for noticing your own default settings, not as a score or a label for you or anyone else. No study measuring the intercultural development of Minnesotans, state employees or DHS staff was found. So this course cannot tell you where Minnesotans "are." It can only invite you to look.

A good first step is small. Start noticing the moments when "normal" turns out to mean "how we do it here."

## Try it

:::scenario
Example for discussion. This is a composite written for teaching, not a real case.
At a DSD team meeting, Sam, who moved to Minnesota from another state six months ago, proposes a new way to schedule follow-up calls with families. A longtime team member, Karen, says, "Well, that's different," and the meeting moves on. After the meeting, Sam tells you he is glad the team liked his idea and plans to start next week. You have worked with Karen for years, and you suspect she has doubts she did not say out loud.
? What do you do?
- Say nothing. Karen will raise her concerns if they matter, and it is not your place to step in. || This may protect everyone from an awkward moment today. It may also leave Sam acting on a meaning he could not read, and Karen's concern may surface later as quiet resistance. Silence can feel neutral from inside the culture while it leaves a newcomer outside it.
- Tell Sam, "Around here, 'that's different' usually means 'no.' I'd drop it." || This may help Sam learn a local code, which is a real kindness. It also assumes you know what Karen meant, and it may end a useful idea before anyone has said why. One pattern does not describe one person, and the decoding is still a guess.
- Check in with Karen privately: "I wasn't sure how you meant 'that's different.' Sam heard it as a yes. Would you be willing to tell him what you're thinking?" || This may help both of them. It treats the phrase as a cultural habit rather than a fault, and it invites Karen to say her view plainly to the person who needs it. It also gives Sam real feedback instead of a code to crack.
:::

## Reflect

:::reflect
- What did "being polite" mean in the home I grew up in? What was I taught not to talk about?
- What is one habit I could practice this month to notice the water I swim in?
:::

## Take away

:::takeaway
This week, notice one moment at work when "normal" was really "how we do it here." It might be a phrase, a meeting habit or a line on a form. Write it down, and ask who might experience it differently.
:::

modules.title: Minnesota nice, decoded
modules.goal: Understand the warmth, the indirectness and the newcomer freeze of Minnesota nice, and how each can look to people from other cultures.
modules.body:
## Opening

Here is a piece of Minnesota humor, and Minnesotans wrote it about themselves.

In 1987, Howard Mohr, a writer for *A Prairie Home Companion*, published *How to Talk Minnesotan: A Visitor's Guide* ([MPR News, Sept. 6, 2022](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2022/09/06/author-howard-mohr-known-for-how-to-talk-minnesotan-dies)). One of its lessons is the "Minnesota Long Goodbye." The visit is over. Everyone says so. Then it goes on in the front hall, then on the steps, and it ends only with the guests in the car and the hosts bent at the driver's window ([Duluth News Tribune via Echo Press, Sept. 6, 2022](https://www.echopress.com/lifestyle/arts-and-entertainment/front-row-seat-remembering-howard-mohr-and-how-to-talk-minnesotan)).

If you smiled, you probably know the rules. Nobody taught them in a class.

This module looks at those rules with affection and with honesty. "Minnesota nice" has a warm side that is real and worth keeping. It also has a guarded side that can be hard to read if you did not grow up with it. In a state that is changing fast, and in work that serves families from many cultures, both sides matter.

## The warm side is real

Start with what is good, because it is not a myth.

Rachel Hutton, a Star Tribune culture reporter, told NPR in 2024 that Minnesotans are "literally nice." She meant kind and polite, the sort of people who will help push a stranger's car out of a snowbank ([NPR, Aug. 9, 2024](https://www.npr.org/transcripts/nx-s1-5065632)).

There is data behind the civic side of that picture.

:::fact
In 2023, 40.3 percent of Minnesotans 16 and older said they had volunteered in the past year, third among the states, against 28.3 percent nationally ([America's Health Rankings, volunteerism, from the Census Bureau's Current Population Survey](https://www.americashealthrankings.org/explore/measures/volunteerism_d/MN)).
:::

Minnesotans also give and take part. Samuel Myers Jr., a University of Minnesota economist, describes a "sustained and vigorous corporate giving culture" in the state ([Humphrey School, The Minnesota Paradox](https://www.hhh.umn.edu/research-centers/roy-wilkins-center-human-relations-and-social-justice/minnesota-paradox)). In 2024, 76.35 percent of eligible Minnesotans voted, second only to Wisconsin. Minnesotans 18 to 29 voted at the highest rate in the nation, 62 percent ([KSTP, citing the Minnesota Secretary of State](https://kstp.com/kstp-news/local-news/minnesotans-ranked-2nd-in-voter-turnout-1st-among-young-voters/)).

Even people who are critical of Minnesota nice grant the warmth. An immigration attorney who moved here told MPR in 2012 that she had seen the state's "collective good will" toward people in need ([MPR News, March 12, 2012](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2012/03/12/outsiders1-is-minnesota-nice-to-newcomers)).

:::voice
"I know someone will write the check." An immigration attorney, on Minnesota's generosity ([MPR News, March 12, 2012](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2012/03/12/outsiders1-is-minnesota-nice-to-newcomers)).
:::

Her next point was the harder one. She was not sure how good Minnesotans were at making refugees "really feel Minnesotan" ([MPR News, March 12, 2012](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2012/03/12/outsiders1-is-minnesota-nice-to-newcomers)). Generosity and distance, side by side: that pairing runs through the rest of this module.

## Reading the code

Mohr's book is humor, but it is humor by a close observer. A Kirkus review summed up the place it describes: things "could be worse," poetry should rhyme, and an offer of help is refused three times before it is accepted ([Kirkus Reviews](https://www.kirkusreviews.com/book-reviews/howard-mohr/how-to-talk-minnesotan-a-visitors-guide/)).

Writing after Mohr's death in 2022, Jay Gabler recalled more of the lessons ([Duluth News Tribune via Echo Press, Sept. 6, 2022](https://www.echopress.com/lifestyle/arts-and-entertainment/front-row-seat-remembering-howard-mohr-and-how-to-talk-minnesotan)):

- "That's different" works as "a blanket reply on neutral ground."
- One lesson is called "The Power of the Negative."
- A guest must refuse food, and the host must insist.

Gabler also named the book's limits. It described how "a certain, then culturally dominant, strain" of Minnesotans talked, not all Minnesotans ([Duluth News Tribune via Echo Press, Sept. 6, 2022](https://www.echopress.com/lifestyle/arts-and-entertainment/front-row-seat-remembering-howard-mohr-and-how-to-talk-minnesotan)). That is worth keeping in mind. Many Minnesotans of every background use these habits, and many do not.

Journalists describe the same code today. Hutton told NPR that if you disliked someone's hotdish at a potluck, you might call it "different" or "interesting" while quietly scraping it into the trash. She added that calling someone "weird," in Minnesota speech, is a harsh statement. Corey Bonnema, co-author of a guide for transplants, described a relative who asks "is it hot in here" instead of asking for the air conditioning ([NPR, Aug. 9, 2024](https://www.npr.org/transcripts/nx-s1-5065632)).

Notice what these moves have in common. The words carry less than the meaning. "Interesting" may mean "I don't like it." "Is it hot in here" means "please turn on the air." A first "no" may mean "ask me again." The listener is expected to read the setting and fill in the rest.

For someone raised in the code, this is smooth and polite. For a coworker, client or family member from somewhere else, including another part of the United States, it can be a puzzle. They may take "that's interesting" as real interest. They may take a first "no, I'm fine" at face value. Or they may sense that something is being left unsaid and not know what.

## When nice avoids conflict

The guarded side of Minnesota nice is the one Minnesotans joke about most.

Hutton described "a habit of understatement" and a tendency, "instead of being direct," to be passive-aggressive. Jerilyn Veldof, Bonnema's co-author, told NPR that passive aggressiveness is what gives the phrase "Minnesota nice" its double meaning ([NPR, Aug. 9, 2024](https://www.npr.org/transcripts/nx-s1-5065632)).

Danielle Lavin-Loucks, a sociologist who grew up in Stillwater and now teaches at Valparaiso University, wrote about this in 2020 ([The Society Pages, July 3, 2020](https://thesocietypages.org/specials/rethinking-minnesota-nice/)).

:::voice
"Avoidance of conflict is central." Danielle Lavin-Loucks, sociologist ([The Society Pages, July 3, 2020](https://thesocietypages.org/specials/rethinking-minnesota-nice/)).
:::

In her description, the things to avoid are visible conflict, open disagreement, un-nice topics and complaints. The tools are a smile, a nod and a change of subject, often to the weather. To others, she writes, that response "appears like agreement" ([The Society Pages, July 3, 2020](https://thesocietypages.org/specials/rethinking-minnesota-nice/)).

That is one person's reflective essay, not a study. But her point matters a great deal at work. In a meeting, silence and a nod can look like a yes. In a reply to a family, a warm tone can look like an answer. Neither is always what it seems.

## Friendly, but hard to befriend

In 2012, MPR's "Outsiders" series heard from dozens of people who had moved to Minnesota. Many found the locals friendly but hard to befriend. Some said their only friends were other transplants ([MPR News, March 12, 2012](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2012/03/12/outsiders1-is-minnesota-nice-to-newcomers)).

:::voice
Minnesotans "will give you directions to anywhere except their own house." A newcomer from Fargo ([MPR News, March 12, 2012](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2012/03/12/outsiders1-is-minnesota-nice-to-newcomers)).
:::

Todd Klingel, then president of the Minneapolis Regional Chamber of Commerce and a lifelong Minnesotan, said the chamber's focus groups with newcomers told stories he found horrifying. He said feelings of isolation were even more common among professionals of color. He also offered a self-test: who have I invited into my house in the last year that I did not know five years ago? MPR noted that Seattle has a similar reputation, so this is not only a Minnesota pattern ([MPR News, March 12, 2012](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2012/03/12/outsiders1-is-minnesota-nice-to-newcomers)).

Grace Vieth, a University of Minnesota researcher, explained the pattern in 2023 as a preference for long-term friendships. Many locals are willing to be friendly but do not follow up, because their existing friends already meet their social needs ([University of Minnesota, 2023](https://cla.umn.edu/psychology/news-events/story/vieth-navigating-social-isolation-newcomer-minnesota)).

None of these sources measured friendship across the state. They describe a reputation that many newcomers recognize. No statewide study measuring Minnesotans' friendliness, indirectness or welcome to newcomers has been found.

## What research shows, and a question

Is there harder evidence? A little, and it comes with cautions.

**Personality by state.** In a 2013 study, Peter Rentfrow and colleagues analyzed samples totaling more than 1.5 million people and mapped average personality traits by state ([Rentfrow et al., 2013, American Psychological Association](https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/releases/psp-a0034434.pdf)).

:::fact
Minnesota's average agreeableness score, 61.6, ranked sixth of 49 listed, among the highest. Its openness score, 38.5, ranked 44th of 49, among the lowest ([Rentfrow et al., 2013, appendix](https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/releases/psp-a0034434.pdf)).
:::

In plain terms, the data fit the "nice" part of the reputation: agreeable and considerate, on average. They also add something the reputation does not always mention, a lower average taste for novelty and change. The authors say their labels give "only a broad sense" of the patterns, and most of the data came from people who chose to take online personality tests ([Rentfrow et al., 2013](https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/releases/psp-a0034434.pdf)).

**Rules and their enforcement.** Jesse Harrington and Michele Gelfand ranked the 50 states on "tightness," meaning many strongly enforced rules and little tolerance for deviance. Minnesota ranked 28th, near the middle ([Harrington and Gelfand, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2014, via PubMed Central](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4050535/)). Their index was built from laws and punishments. It may miss norms that are enforced by quiet disapproval rather than by law. That is a question, not a finding.

**High and low context, as a question.** The anthropologist Edward T. Hall described two styles of communication. In high-context communication, much of the meaning sits in the setting, the relationship and what goes unsaid. In low-context communication, meaning is put into explicit words. An open college textbook, summarizing Hall, places the United States and most of Northern Europe at the low-context end, with the principle "say what you mean" ([Kirkwood Community College open textbook, Cultural Dimensions – Hall](https://kirkwood.pressbooks.pub/emcworthy/chapter/cultural-dimensions/)). The business researcher Erin Meyer calls the United States "the lowest-context culture in the world," as a 2020 article on her work reports ([Welcome to the Jungle, June 1, 2020](https://www.welcometothejungle.com/en-GB/articles/keys-managing-multicultural-teams)).

Yet "that's different," "is it hot in here" and a "no" that means "ask me again" are high-context moves. So here is a question, not an answer: does mainstream Minnesota speech run more high-context among insiders than the national label suggests? And could that help explain why newcomers find it hard to read?

Two cautions. A 2011 review of research using Hall's idea found most country labels rest on "seemingly less-than-adequate evidence" ([Kittler, Rygl and Mackinnon, 2011, University of Stirling repository](https://www.stir.ac.uk/research/hub/publication/818365)). And no study measuring context in Minnesota speech has been found.

Meyer also places Americans in the middle on giving negative feedback. In her account, they are trained to wrap criticism in praise ([Welcome to the Jungle, summarizing Meyer](https://www.welcometothejungle.com/en-GB/articles/keys-managing-multicultural-teams)). If Minnesota leans even gentler, a supervisor's concern may be wrapped so softly that a colleague from a more direct culture does not hear it at all. A colleague from a less direct culture may still hear it as harsh. That is a hypothesis to test in your own workplace.

Use these frameworks as mirrors. Each one describes averages, not people. They are most useful for noticing your own default settings, and least useful as labels for anyone else.

## Try it

:::scenario
Example for discussion. This is a composite written for teaching, not a real case.
Dana works in a DSD program area that answers questions from families. A mother writes: "I have called three times in two weeks. Nobody has called back. My son's services stopped on the 1st. I want to know who is responsible and when this will be fixed." Dana checks and learns the services stopped because a form was not processed, and that a fix may take another week. A coworker suggests a reply that thanks her warmly, says the team "is looking into it," and wishes her a good weekend.
? How might Dana respond?
- Send the coworker's warm reply as written. || This may feel kind and safe, and it avoids naming a mistake. But the mother asked two direct questions, and this reply answers neither. To someone used to plain speech, warmth without an answer may read as a brush-off, and it may lead to a fourth call and less trust.
- Reply plainly and kindly: acknowledge the missed calls, explain that a form was not processed, give the expected timeline, and name who will follow up and when. || This may be uncomfortable, because it states a problem out loud. It also answers what she asked, in words she does not have to decode. Pairing honesty with courtesy uses the best of Minnesota nice instead of its guarded side.
- Call the mother first, ask what she most needs to know, then follow up in writing with the facts and a timeline. || This may build trust, since a call can show care that a written reply cannot. It works best if Dana still says the hard part clearly on the call and does not let a friendly conversation stand in for the answer. The written follow-up may help her keep the facts.
:::

## Reflect

:::reflect
- When I say "that's interesting" or "that's different" at work, what do I mean, and would a colleague from another background hear it that way?
- When a meeting ends with no objections, how do I know whether people agreed?
- Whose feedback do I find hardest to hear: feedback that is too blunt, or too gentle? What does that tell me about my own cultural settings?
:::

## Take away

:::takeaway
This week, say one "no" or one concern plainly and kindly. For example, in your next reply to a family or coworker, answer the direct question in the first sentence, then add the warmth.
:::

modules.title: Where it comes from
modules.goal: Trace mainstream Minnesota culture to its roots in settlement, faith, farm life, climate and civic tradition, so that its everyday habits can be seen as one inheritance among many.
modules.body:
## Opening

Picture a funeral lunch in a church basement in a small Minnesota town. Long tables, folding chairs, coffee in a big urn, bars on paper plates and at least three kinds of hotdish. Nobody sent a sign-up sheet. People just knew what to bring.

That scene has a history. MNopedia, the Minnesota Historical Society's encyclopedia, traces the earliest known hotdish recipe to a 1930 cookbook from a Lutheran church women's society in Mankato. After World War II, it says, the dish moved "out of the church rec room" into home kitchens, served at showers, funerals and rallies as a way to express care ([MNopedia, Hotdish](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/thing/hotdish-mnopedia)).

So a casserole that many of us think of as just "food" grew out of particular churches, particular immigrants and a particular way of showing care. This module asks the same question about the habits we bring to work. They feel natural. They also came from somewhere.

## Settlers, churches and keeping your head down

A culture is partly a set of answers that earlier people worked out to the problems they faced. Mainstream Minnesota culture carries answers worked out by settlers, farmers, church members and organizers more than a century ago.

The story begins with land. MNopedia describes the state's origins as "primarily about the taking of land" from Native people, through treaties, treaty violations and the aftermath of the US-Dakota War of 1862 ([MNopedia, Land, Labor, the Market, and Politics](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/land-labor-market-and-politics)). The settlement story that follows began on land that was taken, and an honest account says so.

Germans were the state's largest single ethnic group by 1917 ([MNopedia, Anti-German Nativism, 1917–1919](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/anti-german-nativism-1917-1919)). Hundreds of thousands of Norwegians arrived between 1851 and 1920, often as whole families who meant to stay, and many settled near one another because they feared extreme isolation ([MNopedia, Norwegian Immigration to Minnesota](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/norwegian-immigration-minnesota)). More Swedes settled in Minnesota than in any other state. Their churches, mostly Lutheran, were "hubs for social as well as religious activities," places that countered isolation and offered help ([MNopedia, Swedish Immigration to Minnesota](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/swedish-immigration-minnesota)).

The church was school, social club and aid society, and later a social service agency. That is one reason so much help in Minnesota still flows through organizations. Today 22 percent of Minnesota adults belong to mainline Protestant churches and 18 percent are Catholic, though many others claim no religion ([Pew Research Center, Religious Landscape Study, Minnesota](https://www.pewresearch.org/religious-landscape-study/state/minnesota/)). The habits these churches formed may outlast their hold.

The majority culture also learned to keep its head down. During World War I, a state commission with what MNopedia calls "near-dictatorial powers" watched German Americans closely, and officials in New Ulm who questioned the draft were removed from office ([MNopedia, Anti-German Nativism](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/anti-german-nativism-1917-1919)). Swedish Lutheran churches moved to English services in the 1920s and 1930s, hastened in part by pressure to Americanize ([MNopedia, Swedish Immigration](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/swedish-immigration-minnesota)). Whether some of today's caution about standing out was learned in those years is a fair question. No source in the essay answers it.

Many Minnesotans point to a Scandinavian source for that caution. In a 2009 MPR essay, playwright Syl Jones traced Minnesota nice to the "Jante law," the unwritten rules of a fictional town in a 1930s novel by Aksel Sandemose, which begin "Don't think that you are special" ([MPR News, Dec. 14, 2009](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2009/12/14/syljones)).

:::voice
Syl Jones argued that Minnesota nice is "more about keeping up appearances" than niceness ([MPR News, 2009](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2009/12/14/syljones)).
:::

That is one writer's essay, not a study. It describes a novel's town, not measured Minnesotans. It is worth knowing because so many people find it familiar.

The usual story of roots also leaves people out: the Dakota and Ojibwe people whose land this was, the Black Minnesotans of St. Paul's Rondo neighborhood and north Minneapolis, and Mexican farmworkers, about 7,000 of whom worked the sugar beet fields as early as 1928 ([MNopedia, Land, Labor, the Market, and Politics](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/land-labor-market-and-politics)). A culture's picture of itself is a selection.

## Farms, winters and cooperatives

Where did Minnesota nice come from? University of St. Thomas sociologist Lisa Waldner told MPR in 2019 that there is no definitive documentation. She offered two likely threads. Northern European settlers clustered by group, so that people lived side by side without mixing much. And on a farm you might need a neighbor's help when your plow broke at harvest, so politeness won out over hostility ([MPR News, Nov. 21, 2019](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2019/11/21/ask-a-sotan-revisiting-minnesota-nice)).

:::voice
Of early settlers, Lisa Waldner said people "co-existed, but you didn't intermingle" ([MPR News, 2019](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2019/11/21/ask-a-sotan-revisiting-minnesota-nice)).
:::

Waldner's account holds two values in tension: a strong ethic of handling your own problems, and a practical dependence on the people nearby.

Winter belongs in the story too. Writer Jay Gabler summarized humorist Howard Mohr's view that Minnesota sociability rests on a stoicism born of the need to outlast brutal winters ([Duluth News Tribune via Echo Press, Sept. 6, 2022](https://www.echopress.com/lifestyle/arts-and-entertainment/front-row-seat-remembering-howard-mohr-and-how-to-talk-minnesotan)). That is humor by a close observer, not research. University of Minnesota researcher Grace Vieth has linked newcomers' isolation partly to long winters, when people stay with the friends they already have ([University of Minnesota Department of Psychology, Sept. 2023](https://cla.umn.edu/psychology/news-events/story/vieth-navigating-social-isolation-newcomer-minnesota)).

Minnesota's habit of solving problems together has a concrete history. In 1890 the Danish American community at Clarks Grove founded one of the state's first cooperative creameries. For decades the creamery was also a community center, hosting talks, meetings and school recitals ([MNopedia, Clarks Grove Cooperative Creamery](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/group/clarks-grove-cooperative-creamery)).

:::fact
By 1928, nearly half of all the cooperative creameries in the United States were in Minnesota ([MNopedia, Clarks Grove Cooperative Creamery](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/group/clarks-grove-cooperative-creamery)).
:::

Pooling resources, sharing profits and losses, and meeting to decide are habits with deep roots here.

## Government as a shared moral project

The political scientist Daniel Elazar described three American political cultures. In the "individualistic" one, politics is a marketplace and a career. In the "traditionalistic" one, an established elite governs. In the "moralistic" one, politics is a shared search for the good society, government is "a positive instrument" for the general welfare, and public service carries moral duties. Elazar called Minnesota "the archetypical example" of the moralistic culture and traced it to Yankee settlers reinforced by Scandinavian and German immigrants ([Daniel J. Elazar, "Minnesota: The Epitome of the Moralistic Political Culture"](https://dje.jcpa.org/articles2/minn3.htm)). In his view, Minnesotans argue about how large a role government should play, not whether it should play one.

Treat this framework as a mirror, not a label. It is one scholar's classification, built from settlement history rather than surveys, and it describes a state's public life, not any person in it. Elazar himself named a tension that matters for a large agency: the moralistic culture has a "major difficulty with bureaucracy," and where merit systems exist, "they tend to be rigidly maintained" ([Elazar](https://dje.jcpa.org/articles2/minn3.htm)).

The history behind the framework is real. The Farmer-Labor Party grew from farmers' and workers' organizing against monopolies and elected hundreds of candidates from 1917 into the 1940s ([MNopedia, Minnesota Farmer-Labor Party, 1924–1944](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/minnesota-farmer-labor-party-1924-1944)). In 1948 Hubert Humphrey urged his party to "walk forthrightly in the bright sunshine of human rights" ([MNopedia, Hubert H. Humphrey](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/person/humphrey-hubert-h-1911-1978)). The 1967 state civil rights law passed with support from both parties ([MNopedia, Minnesota Human Rights Act](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/thing/minnesota-human-rights-act)). The 1971 "Minnesota Miracle," which shifted most school costs to the state, took the longest special session in state history. Before it, the richest districts had the lowest tax rates and the highest spending per pupil ([MNopedia, Minnesota Miracle](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/thing/minnesota-miracle-legislation)).

:::fact
In 2024, 76.35 percent of eligible Minnesotans voted, second in the nation, and young Minnesotans' turnout ranked first ([KSTP, citing the Minnesota Secretary of State](https://kstp.com/kstp-news/local-news/minnesotans-ranked-2nd-in-voter-turnout-1st-among-young-voters/)).
:::

This picture is not the whole present. Hamline political scientist David Schultz argued in a 2025 column that "the myth of Minnesota exceptionalism" no longer holds, describing a swing state with sharp regional divides ([Duluth News Tribune, June 26, 2025](https://www.duluthnewstribune.com/opinion/columns/state-view-minnesota-exceptionalism-it-turns-out-was-a-myth)). Easy consensus is part of the inheritance, but not a promise.

## Values under the surface

Values are the beliefs about what is good that sit underneath behavior. Here are five that the history above helps explain. Each is a strength. Each can also hide something.

**Self-reliance, with organized help.** Farm history, and a 2013 personality study's finding of high average conscientiousness across the wider north central region, point to a culture that values steady work and handling one's own problems ([Rentfrow et al., 2013](https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/releases/psp-a0034434.pdf)). Yet cooperatives and church aid societies show a strong habit of helping. In the essay's reading, help here is often organized through institutions, and given more easily than it is asked for.

**Egalitarianism and "treat everyone the same."** Business researcher Erin Meyer places Scandinavian countries among the most egalitarian on her leading scale ([Welcome to the Jungle, summarizing Meyer](https://www.welcometothejungle.com/en-GB/articles/keys-managing-multicultural-teams)). Minnesota's civic tradition prizes fairness too. The difficulty is that fairness can mean identical treatment, or treatment that gets people to the same place. That question returns in Module 6.

**Modesty and privacy.** Jones's essay and Mohr's humor both describe a culture that discourages standing out ([MPR News, 2009](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2009/12/14/syljones); [Duluth News Tribune via Echo Press, 2022](https://www.echopress.com/lifestyle/arts-and-entertainment/front-row-seat-remembering-howard-mohr-and-how-to-talk-minnesotan)). A culture that keeps its troubles private may also find it awkward to ask others about theirs, which matters in work that depends on asking.

**Consensus and trust in process.** The bipartisan rights law and the Minnesota Miracle show a culture that trusts long process to reach fair results ([MNopedia, Minnesota Miracle](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/thing/minnesota-miracle-legislation)). Meyer notes that consensus decisions "take much longer to reach" but are harder to change ([Welcome to the Jungle, summarizing Meyer](https://www.welcometothejungle.com/en-GB/articles/keys-managing-multicultural-teams)). Trust in institutions is a strength. It can be a blind spot with people whose own or family history gives them reason to trust less.

None of these values is "Minnesotan" in the sense of belonging to every Minnesotan, and none is measured for Minnesota alone. They are inherited defaults. Knowing their history lets you choose when to lean on them and when to set them aside.

## Try it
:::scenario
Example for discussion. This is a composite written for teaching, not a real case.
Dana joined your DSD unit three months ago after years working for a state agency in the South. After a team meeting she tells you what puzzles her: no one took credit when a project went well, a coworker turned down help twice before accepting it, and a small policy change has now been discussed in four meetings "until everyone is on board." She asks you, "Why does everyone here work this way?"
? How might you respond?
- "Honestly, that's just how professional teams work. You'll get used to it." || This may reassure Dana that nothing is wrong. It may also present local habits as the universal standard, which is the "water" this course asks us to notice, and it leaves her as the one who must adjust.
- "Some of that may be Minnesota habits. Modesty, refusing help at first and slow consensus all have local history, from church and farm life to cooperatives. How did your old team handle these things?" || This may help Dana see the habits as learned values rather than rules, and it names their roots without claiming they fit everyone. Asking about her old team treats her experience as equally valid and may show you something about your own defaults.
- "Ha, that's Minnesota nice. Don't take it personally." || This may put Dana at ease with shared humor, and it is kind. It may also bundle three different habits under one joke, so the values behind them stay out of view, and it does not invite her to say what she would find helpful.
:::

## Reflect
:::reflect
- When I think "I treat everyone the same," what is the "same" based on? Whose way of doing things is the default?
- What strengths of Minnesota culture do I bring to my work, and how could I use them more deliberately with people whose culture differs from mine?
:::

## Take away
:::takeaway
This week, name one value you hold at work, such as waiting for consensus or not asking for help, and trace it to where you learned it: a church basement, a family farm, a first supervisor. Write the pair down where you will see it.
:::

## Go deeper
- Essay, section 3: Roots of mainstream Minnesota culture
- Essay, section 7: Political culture
- Essay, section 9: Values under the surface
- Essay, section 15: Strengths to build on

modules.title: Seen from the other side
modules.goal: Hear how Minnesota's majority culture is experienced by Minnesotans of color, immigrants and newcomers, and face the state's racial history honestly.
modules.body:
## Opening

Here is a line that gets a knowing laugh, and it is meant as humor. A newcomer from Fargo told MPR News about being warned Minnesotans "will give you directions to anywhere except their own house" ([MPR News, March 12, 2012](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2012/03/12/outsiders1-is-minnesota-nice-to-newcomers)).

Most of us who grew up here can laugh at that, because we know the person giving those directions. They are friendly. They are helpful. They mean well. And they may not notice that the newcomer drove away still feeling like a guest.

That small joke points to something larger. A culture looks one way from the inside and another way from the outside. The people inside it often see kindness. People arriving from elsewhere, or people the culture has kept at a distance, may see something more mixed.

This module listens to those outside views. It also looks at parts of Minnesota's racial history that the majority culture has not always talked about. The goal is not to feel bad about home. It is to see home more completely.

## Voices from outside the majority

Many of the sharpest observations about Minnesota's majority culture come from people who stand partly outside it. None of them speaks for a whole community.

In a 2002 MPR documentary, Arthur McWatt, a St. Paul native and retired social studies teacher, described employers who accepted a Black applicant's application and then threw it away. He called it discrimination "done in a more subtle way than in the South." He said Black Minnesotans learned that racist white people often had smiling faces and polite voices, and developed "an antenna" for insincerity. He also said Black Minnesotans generally felt safer here than in the South ([MPR, "Up South," Feb. 12, 2002](https://archive.mpr.org/stories/2002/02/12/african-americans-jim-crow-north)).

:::voice
Ken Charles, a General Mills executive, said a job gets newcomers "the 9 to 5," and "the harder part is the 5 to 9" ([MPR News, March 12, 2012](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2012/03/12/outsiders1-is-minnesota-nice-to-newcomers)).
:::

That same 2012 MPR series reported that professionals of color who moved to the Twin Cities often said locals "accept them, but lack a genuine understanding of other cultures." The same story carried a refugee's very different view: Minnesotans welcomed him and gave him a job before he spoke English well, and "I think I can say that's nice" ([MPR News, March 12, 2012](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2012/03/12/outsiders1-is-minnesota-nice-to-newcomers)). Both experiences are real.

Some voices come from inside the majority, looking back. Danielle Lavin-Loucks, a sociologist who grew up in Stillwater in the 1970s, wrote that her family stressed that "people are people." By not talking about race, she did not really see it. She now sees that kind of colorblindness as discounting the experiences of people of color ([The Society Pages, July 3, 2020](https://thesocietypages.org/specials/rethinking-minnesota-nice/)). University of St. Thomas sociologist Lisa Waldner described a white Minnesotan who reasons that being polite to everyone means there are no issues around race. She said she does not think the intent is malicious, but called it a form of denial that can sustain institutional racism in housing and education ([MPR News, Nov. 21, 2019](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2019/11/21/ask-a-sotan-revisiting-minnesota-nice)).

Immigrant and refugee participants in a 2021 Twin Cities planning effort on belonging voiced frustration at "over-engagement": being asked for input again and again without seeing it in the final product ([The Journey to Belonging in the Twin Cities, City of Saint Paul, 2022](https://www.stpaul.gov/sites/default/files/2022-04/The%20Journey%20to%20Belonging%20in%20the%20Twin%20Cities%20Report.pdf)). For a public agency, that one deserves a long pause.

These voices do not say Minnesotans are unkind. Most say the opposite. What they describe is a culture in which kindness and avoidance can look the same from inside, and very different from outside.

## The Minnesota paradox

Samuel Myers Jr., director of the Roy Wilkins Center at the University of Minnesota's Humphrey School, calls it "the Minnesota Paradox." Minnesota is one of the best places to live in America. Yet by racial gaps in unemployment, income, incarceration, homeownership, test scores, school discipline and more, African Americans are worse off here than in "virtually every other state" ([Humphrey School](https://www.hhh.umn.edu/research-centers/roy-wilkins-center-human-relations-and-social-justice/minnesota-paradox)).

There is a nuance worth holding. A 2020 WCCO report noted that many indicators for Black Minnesotans are not worse than elsewhere. The gaps are wide partly because white Minnesotans do better than average ([CBS Minnesota, June 23, 2020](https://www.cbsnews.com/minnesota/news/the-minnesota-paradox-why-the-land-of-10000-lakes-has-one-of-the-largest-racial-disparities/)).

:::voice
Samuel Myers Jr. described Minnesota's racism as the kind "where people say there is no racism" ([CBS Minnesota, June 23, 2020](https://www.cbsnews.com/minnesota/news/the-minnesota-paradox-why-the-land-of-10000-lakes-has-one-of-the-largest-racial-disparities/)).
:::

Myers also names a habit worth watching for. He writes that in the 1990s, "in a characteristically Minnesotan manner," leaders blamed rising problems in the Black community on migrants from Chicago, Detroit and Gary, so the problem was "not Minnesota" ([Humphrey School](https://www.hhh.umn.edu/research-centers/roy-wilkins-center-human-relations-and-social-justice/minnesota-paradox)). He sees the same move in claims after 2020 that outside agitators drove the unrest. The pattern he describes, placing a problem outside the group so the group's self-image stays intact, is common in many dominant cultures. It is a mirror, not a verdict: you can ask whether you have ever reached for it yourself.

## A history kept out of view

Minnesota's racial history is often less visible than the South's, and that is part of the story.

**Racial covenants.** Starting in 1910, Minneapolis developers wrote racial covenants into property deeds, barring sale or rental to people of Black, Asian and other descent. By the 1930s most new residential developments in the Twin Cities carried them. The legislature banned them in 1953. MNopedia notes they sat "out of view" in county deed books, in places "imagined to be free from Jim Crow" ([MNopedia, Racial Housing Covenants in the Twin Cities](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/thing/racial-housing-covenants-twin-cities)). The University of Minnesota's Mapping Prejudice project maps these deeds with community volunteers ([Mapping Prejudice, University of Minnesota](https://mappingprejudice.umn.edu/)). A 2019 state law lets homeowners formally discharge a covenant, though the project explains this does not erase what it calls "the receipts of structural racism" ([Mapping Prejudice, discharging racial covenants](https://mappingprejudice.umn.edu/discharging-racial-covenants)). Myers traces today's homeownership gaps partly to these policies ([Humphrey School](https://www.hhh.umn.edu/research-centers/roy-wilkins-center-human-relations-and-social-justice/minnesota-paradox)).

**Rondo and I-94.** St. Paul's Rondo neighborhood was the center of Black life in the city, with its own clubs, a credit union and a cooperative ([MNopedia, Rondo Neighborhood](https://www3.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/place/rondo-neighborhood-st-paul)). Interstate 94, built between 1956 and 1968, cut it in half.

:::fact
In Rondo, 600 families lost their homes to Interstate 94 ([MNopedia, Neighborhood Resistance to I-94](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/event/neighborhood-resistance-i-94-1953-1965)).
:::

MNopedia compares Rondo with mostly white, professional Merriam Park, where well-connected residents won several changes. In Rondo, it concludes, a "lack of political clout, along with racial and class bias, left Rondo vulnerable" ([MNopedia, Neighborhood Resistance to I-94](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/event/neighborhood-resistance-i-94-1953-1965)). For anyone who works in public process, the lesson is pointed. A process can be open to everyone and still respond most to people who already know how it works.

**Schools.** Minnesota's graduation rate reached a record 85 percent for the class of 2025, with gains among Black, Asian and Native American students and students in special education ([MPR News, April 3, 2026](https://www.mprnews.org/story/2026/04/03/minnesota-graduation-rates-hit-record-high-in-2025)). Even so, Hamline University political scientist David Schultz wrote in 2025 that outcomes for students of color "are among the nation's worst" ([Duluth News Tribune, June 26, 2025](https://www.duluthnewstribune.com/opinion/columns/state-view-minnesota-exceptionalism-it-turns-out-was-a-myth)). Scholars disagree about the causes. Myron Orfield of the University of Minnesota Law School has argued that ending desegregation efforts made gaps worse, while Myers does not see housing segregation as the main cause ([CBS Minnesota, 2020](https://www.cbsnews.com/minnesota/news/the-minnesota-paradox-why-the-land-of-10000-lakes-has-one-of-the-largest-racial-disparities/)).

:::note
Content note: This passage describes the 1920 lynchings in Duluth. Readers may pause or skip to the next section.
:::

**Duluth, 1920.** On June 15, 1920, three Black circus workers, Elias Clayton, Elmer Jackson and Isaac McGhie, were lynched by a mob in Duluth after a white couple accused six Black circus workers of robbery and rape. A doctor who examined the young woman found no evidence of rape. No one was convicted of murder ([MNopedia, Duluth Lynchings](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/event/duluth-lynchings)). MNopedia notes that lynching "is widely believed to be something that happened only in the South." The lynchings were then "mostly forgotten or ignored" until 1991, when the men's graves received headstones. A memorial and an annual day of remembrance followed ([MNopedia, Duluth Lynchings](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/event/duluth-lynchings)). The long forgetting is part of the cultural story too.

## 2020: a hard look at culture

:::note
Content note: This section refers to the police killing of George Floyd in 2020 and to findings about police use of force. Readers may pause or skip to the next section.
:::

On May 25, 2020, George Floyd, a 46-year-old Black man, was killed by a Minneapolis police officer during an arrest. Myers opened his account of the Minnesota paradox by asking how this could happen in a state "known for being 'nice'" ([Humphrey School](https://www.hhh.umn.edu/research-centers/roy-wilkins-center-human-relations-and-social-justice/minnesota-paradox)).

In April 2022, the Minnesota Department of Human Rights found probable cause that the City of Minneapolis and its police department had engaged in a pattern of race discrimination. Its findings included more severe force used against Black people than white people in similar circumstances ([Minnesota Department of Human Rights, April 27, 2022](https://mn.gov/mdhr/assets/Investigation%20into%20the%20City%20of%20Minneapolis%20and%20the%20Minneapolis%20Police%20Department_tcm1061-526417.pdf)).

What matters most for this course is the report's main conclusion. The department wrote that the pattern was caused "primarily by an organizational culture," and that without real culture change, new policies and trainings "will be meaningless." It said culture is shaped by the tone leaders set, how norms are taught and reinforced, and what happens when they are broken ([MDHR, 2022](https://mn.gov/mdhr/assets/Investigation%20into%20the%20City%20of%20Minneapolis%20and%20the%20Minneapolis%20Police%20Department_tcm1061-526417.pdf)). The report concerns one police department, and nothing here suggests it describes DHS. But its idea, that culture can outlast policy, applies to any public institution, including ours.

## Repair, equity work and an honest debate

Since 2020, and before, Minnesotans have worked on this history in many ways.

**Repairing the record.** The covenant discharge law, Mapping Prejudice's volunteer mapping, the state's 2020 pardon of Max Mason, a Black man convicted in a case related to the Duluth lynchings, and the work of Duluth's memorial committee all address history directly ([Mapping Prejudice](https://mappingprejudice.umn.edu/discharging-racial-covenants); [MNopedia, Duluth Lynchings](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/event/duluth-lynchings)). Rondo's residents have kept their neighborhood's memory alive through Rondo Days since 1983 ([MNopedia, Rondo](https://www3.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/place/rondo-neighborhood-st-paul)).

**State government.** Executive Order 23-12, signed in 2023, continued the state's diversity and equity councils, noted the appointment of the state's first Chief Equity Officer, and directed agencies to carry out a long-range equity plan ([Executive Order 23-12](https://www.lrl.mn.gov/archive/execorders/23-12.pdf)). An earlier order said a person's opportunities "should not depend on their race, identity, ability," place of origin, place of worship or zip code ([Executive Order 21-13](https://www.lrl.mn.gov/archive/execorders/21-13.pdf)).

**Community-led work.** Much of the most important equity work is led by communities themselves, including newsrooms such as the Minnesota Spokesman-Recorder, which launched an essay series on the paradox in 2024 ([Minnesota Spokesman-Recorder, Nov. 14, 2024](https://spokesman-recorder.com/2024/11/14/minnesota-paradox-black-disparities/)).

**The debate.** Equity work has critics, and their views are part of Minnesota's civic life. In 2021, Catrin Wigfall, a policy fellow at the Center of the American Experiment, argued that equality means equal opportunity, while equity means guaranteeing equal outcomes, which in her view is "at its core, discrimination" ([Post Bulletin, June 8, 2021](https://www.postbulletin.com/news/local/center-for-the-american-experiment-presenters-criticize-use-of-critical-race-theory-in-minnesota-schools)). By 2025, federal executive orders had ended diversity, equity and inclusion programs across the federal government. Minnesota State Chancellor Scott Olson defended his system's equity work, saying "Minnesota needs everybody in the workforce" and describing equity in terms of first-generation and low-income students as well as students of color ([Post Bulletin, Jan. 25, 2025](https://www.postbulletin.com/news/local/dei-is-being-banished-in-government-and-business-but-not-in-higher-education-in-minnesota)).

You do not need to pick a side here. It helps to notice that people of good faith disagree about the words "equity" and "equality," and that the majority culture's habit of "treat everyone the same" sits at the center of that disagreement.

## Try it

:::scenario
Example for discussion. This is a composite written for teaching, not a real case.
Your DSD team just held a meeting with community partners about changes to how families learn about a waiver service. To you, it went smoothly: no one objected, and the group agreed to move ahead. Afterward, your colleague Dana, who is Black and has worked with several of the families involved, tells you she saw it differently. She says two partners went quiet after their first comments were passed over, and she felt her own concern was thanked and then dropped.
? What do you do next?
- Explain what you saw: no one objected, so it seemed like real agreement. || This may feel like reassurance to you, but it can tell Dana that her view counts for less than yours. Sociologist Danielle Lavin-Loucks has written that a smile and a nod can look like agreement when they are not ([The Society Pages, July 3, 2020](https://thesocietypages.org/specials/rethinking-minnesota-nice/)), so your view of the room may be the less complete one.
- Thank her, ask what she noticed, and ask whether the two of you could follow up with the partners who went quiet. || This may take more time, and it may surface concerns the group then has to address. It treats Dana's outside view as information you could not see from where you sat, and it moves toward the people whose voices were lost, not just toward the record of the meeting.
- Thank her and suggest she raise her concern with the meeting lead. || This may respect her voice, and the lead may need to hear it. It may also leave the work of speaking up with the person who already felt passed over. Rondo's history shows that processes tend to respond most to people who already know how to work them, so offering to go with her, or raising it yourself, may help.
:::

## Reflect

:::reflect
- Who have I invited into my home, or my circle at work, in the last year whom I did not know five years ago?
- What did I learn growing up about race in Minnesota, and what did I learn later? Who taught me each?
- When a problem arises in a community, do I look first for causes inside our systems, or outside them?
:::

## Take away

:::takeaway
Seek out one perspective you would not usually hear. This week, ask a colleague, partner or family member from outside your own background how a recent meeting, letter or process looked to them, then listen without explaining what you meant.
:::

- Essay, section 5: How it looks from outside the majority
- Essay, section 6: Race and racism in Minnesota's history and present
- Essay, section 8: Anti-racism and equity work, and the debate about it

modules.title: Culture in the system we run
modules.goal: See how majority-culture values are built into disability policy and practice.
modules.body:
## Opening

Here is a bit of Minnesotans' own humor about themselves. Howard Mohr's 1987 book *How to Talk Minnesotan* described a place where an offer of help is refused three times before it is accepted ([Kirkus Reviews](https://www.kirkusreviews.com/book-reviews/howard-mohr/how-to-talk-minnesotan-a-visitors-guide/)). The guest must refuse the food, and the host must insist ([Duluth News Tribune via Echo Press, Sept. 6, 2022](https://www.echopress.com/lifestyle/arts-and-entertainment/front-row-seat-remembering-howard-mohr-and-how-to-talk-minnesotan)).

It is a joke, but it carries a real pattern. In many Minnesota homes, help is given more easily than it is asked for, and it often comes through institutions: the church, the cooperative, the nonprofit, the state.

Disability services are one of those institutions. We built them, and they carry our habits. That includes our ideas about what help looks like, who should decide, and what a good life is. This module looks at the system we run as a cultural product. That is not a criticism of the system. It is a way to see it more clearly, and to notice the families it fits easily and the ones it fits less well.

## A history we inherited

Disability is not only a service area. It is part of Minnesota's cultural history, and that history still shapes how some people view public agencies.

:::note
Content note: This section describes abuse, neglect, forced sterilization and deaths in state institutions. Readers may pause or skip to the next section.
:::

Minnesota built a system of state institutions for people with disabilities. They included Faribault State School and Hospital, which began in 1879, and the Colony for Epileptics, which opened at Cambridge in 1925 and closed as Cambridge State Hospital in 1997 ([Minnesota Historical Society Library, Institutions for People with Disabilities](https://libguides.mnhs.org/institutions/disabilities)). Over time, such institutions shifted from education to lifelong custodial care. By the 1960s they were overcrowded and understaffed, and families worried about chemical and physical restraints ([MNopedia, Welsch v. Likins](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/event/welsch-v-likins)).

The eugenics laws are a harder part of the story. A 1917 law let county probate judges commit people judged "feeble minded" without their families' consent. Being poor or behaving unusually could count as a sign. MNopedia notes that an immigrant who failed an English-language IQ test could be labeled this way. A 1925 law authorized sterilization ([MNopedia, Eugenics in Minnesota](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/thing/eugenics-minnesota)).

:::fact
At least 2,204 Minnesotans were sterilized between 1925 and 1945, 77 percent of them women. The true number is unknown because no central board kept records ([MNopedia, Eugenics in Minnesota](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/thing/eugenics-minnesota)).
:::

The people behind this saw themselves as reformers. MNopedia describes Charles Dight, founder of the Minnesota Eugenics Society, as "consistently interested in social reform and utopian politics" ([MNopedia, Eugenics in Minnesota](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/thing/eugenics-minnesota)). The lesson for us is not that reform is dangerous. It is that confidence in our own good intentions is not a safeguard.

Families pushed back. The parents of Patricia Welsch, a resident at Cambridge, worked with the Legal Aid Society of Minneapolis and the Arc of Minnesota to bring a class action. In 1974, Judge Earl Larson ruled that residents had a constitutional right to treatment ([MNopedia, Welsch v. Likins](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/event/welsch-v-likins)). The Arc's history credits parents with pressing for the Developmental Disabilities Waiver and helping negotiate the plan to close the state institutions and replace them with community services ([The Arc Minnesota, History of The Arc in Minnesota](https://arcminnesota.org/about/why-the-arc/history-of-the-arc-in-minnesota/)). And around 13,000 people who died in state hospitals were buried in graves marked only with numbers, or nothing. In 1994, disability self-advocates formed Remembering With Dignity to give them named stones ([MNopedia, Remembering With Dignity](https://www.mnhs.org/mnopedia/search/index/group/remembering-dignity)).

Notice the arc of this story. It moves from institutions run *for* people, to parents suing on their behalf, to self-advocates speaking for themselves. The central question shifted from "how do we care for people?" to "who decides?" For a culture proud of helping, that shift can be uncomfortable, because it means sharing control. It is also the shift today's policy rests on.

## Values written into law

Those hard-won lessons are now written into Minnesota law. State policy says adults with disabilities, and children with support from their families, may make "informed choices" about services. The process must give information "in a manner that is culturally and linguistically appropriate" and identify the person's cultural needs ([Minn. Stat. 256B.4905](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/256B.4905)).

The licensing law for home and community-based services requires person-centered planning. It asks what is important "to the person" as well as "for the person," and calls for self-determination and "the most integrated setting" ([Minn. Stat. 245D.07](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/245D.07)). Minnesota's Olmstead Plan aims for disabled Minnesotans to live full, integrated lives in communities of their choosing, as the Metropolitan Center for Independent Living summarizes it ([Metropolitan Center for Independent Living](https://mcil-mn.org/mcil-ada-minnesota-submits-comments-on-education-and-employment-to-minnesota-olmstead-plan/)).

:::voice
The licensing law asks planners to respect "each person's history, dignity, and cultural background" ([Minn. Stat. 245D.07](https://www.revisor.mn.gov/statutes/cite/245D.07)).
:::

These are strong protections, won by disabled people and families. They also carry assumptions that match the majority culture: that the individual is the main decision-maker, that independence is a central goal, and that the most integrated setting is usually best. Seeing these as cultural values, and not simply as "correct," is not a criticism. The law itself names the tension when it requires cultural needs to be identified.

## The same values, seen from other homes

The community profiles in this series document how some families describe disability, care and decision-making. These examples come from particular studies at particular times. They do not describe every member of any community.

In a 2014 Minnesota Department of Health study of families of children with autism, Hmong parents described stigma tied to a belief that families may be "genetically flawed or cursed." A Somali parent described a fear that people would say "it's because of the mother." A Latino parent described a fear that a child would be seen as "crazy" ([Minnesota Department of Health, report to the Legislature, Feb. 15, 2014](https://www.leg.mn.gov/docs/2014/mandated/140404.pdf)). In 2015 community conversations with 220 Somali participants, people described turning first to the mosque, the Quran or spiritual leaders ([Minnesota Department of Health, Somali Mental Health Project](https://www.health.mn.gov/communities/equity/reports/mentalhealth.pdf)). Some Somali parents, professionals and autistic people have since proposed *maangaar*, "unique mind," as a new word for autism ([Sahan Journal, updated April 7, 2026](https://sahanjournal.com/health/autism-somali-new-terminology-community-acceptance-minnesota/)).

Data on service use raises related questions. A 2021 study for DHS compared how racial and ethnic groups in Minnesota's Medicaid population used home and community-based services ([Arling and colleagues, report to DHS, March 26, 2021](https://developtoolmn.org/dhs/assets/racial-and-ethnic-comparison-report-quantatitive_tcm1053-663962.pdf)).

:::fact
Under age 65, 46 percent of white people in the study were on a disability waiver. Asian and Pacific Islander people (38 percent) and Black people (31 percent) most often used personal care assistance without a waiver ([Arling and colleagues, report to DHS, March 26, 2021](https://developtoolmn.org/dhs/assets/racial-and-ethnic-comparison-report-quantatitive_tcm1053-663962.pdf)).
:::

The authors say plainly that they "do not attempt to draw conclusions" about causes ([Arling and colleagues, 2021](https://developtoolmn.org/dhs/assets/racial-and-ethnic-comparison-report-quantatitive_tcm1053-663962.pdf)). So we should not either. Research has not established why these gaps exist in Minnesota.

What these findings do not show is that any community "values independence less." They show differences in where families turn first, how disability is named, who in the family decides and which services get used. Joseph Vandello and Dov Cohen's 1999 index of state individualism even counted older people living alone and grandparents in the household as markers ([Cambridge University Press supplementary material describing the index](https://static.cambridge.org/content/id/urn:cambridge.org:id:article:S0140525X11000021/resource/name/S0140525X11000021sup001.pdf)). A system designed around a person who lives on their own, makes their own choices and works in the community will fit some households more naturally than others. When a family member answers for an adult with a disability, is that a rights problem, a norm the person has chosen, or both? The honest answer is that you have to ask.

## Inside the agency

Culture also shapes how we work with each other. Minnesota Management and Budget's 2025 Employee Engagement and Inclusion Survey asked state employees whether they feel comfortable sharing ideas "even when they differ from others'." 58 percent agreed and another 24 percent somewhat agreed ([MMB, Statewide Employee Engagement and Inclusion Survey, High-Level Employee Statement Results, August 2025](https://mn.gov/mmb-stat/communications/toolkit/2025/employeesurvey/Employee%20Engagement%20and%20Inclusion%20Survey%20Results.pdf)). Roughly four in ten did not fully agree. The public summary does not break results down by agency or group, so it cannot tell us whether DHS differs.

:::voice
Sociologist Danielle Lavin-Loucks writes that a smile and a nod "appears like agreement" ([The Society Pages, 2020](https://thesocietypages.org/specials/rethinking-minnesota-nice/)).
:::

No published study has observed how these habits play out in state agency meetings. Still, the question is worth carrying into your next one: when no one objects, has the group agreed, or have some people decided objecting is not worth the cost?

Recent oversight findings also touch DHS directly. On March 17, 2026, the Office of the Legislative Auditor found that DHS "has long had legal authority" to address alleged kickbacks in the EIDBI autism benefit, though officials had said it lacked that authority before 2025. The auditor also identified a decades-old error in the department's rules that may limit its ability to suspend payments during such investigations ([Office of the Legislative Auditor, special review, March 17, 2026](https://www.auditor.leg.state.mn.us/sreview/2026/dhs-oig-kickbacks.htm)). Separately, DHS ended its Housing Stabilization Services program on October 31, 2025, citing widespread fraud, even though, in the department's words, it "truly filled an important gap" for many participants ([DHS bulletin, Oct. 31, 2025](https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/MNDHS/bulletins/3f98793)).

These findings raise questions without settling them. How does a culture of trust in providers and partners, which serves many people well, notice when that trust is abused? And how does an agency tighten oversight without casting suspicion on whole communities?

## Try it
:::scenario
Example for discussion. This is a composite written for teaching, not a real case.
Maria is a lead agency case manager meeting with Sam, a 24-year-old with a developmental disability, and his parents and older sister. The family says decisions about Sam are made together, and they want him to keep living at home with relatives caring for him. The planning form in front of Maria has sections on independent living goals and competitive employment.
? What could Maria do next?
- Ask the family to step out for part of the meeting so she can hear Sam's own wishes privately. || This may help make sure Sam's voice is heard, which the law and the disability rights history both value. It may also feel to the family like distrust if it comes without explanation. Asking Sam first how he would like decisions made, and who he wants in the room, may honor his choice and the family's way of deciding together.
- Note the family's preference, then walk through each section of the form, presenting supported living and job services as goals to work toward. || This may cover everything the form asks, and the family will hear about real options. It may also signal that care at home is a starting point to move past, not a valid choice. The family may agree politely in the meeting without feeling heard, and the plan may not reflect what they actually want.
- Ask Sam and his family what a good life looks like for him, in their own words, then explain the options in their preferred language and ask how they would like to decide. || This may take longer, and the answers may not fit the form's headings neatly. It treats care at home and shared decision-making as choices worth understanding, while still making sure Sam and his family know every option well enough for the choice to be informed. It may also build trust that carries into future meetings.
:::

## Reflect
:::reflect
- How do I picture a "good outcome" for a person with a disability: living independently, working, making their own choices? Where did that picture come from, and would every family share it?
- When a family wants to make decisions together, or care for someone at home, how do I respond? How does the planning process respond?
- What do I know about the history of Minnesota's state institutions, eugenics laws and racial covenants? How might that history shape the trust a family gives me?
:::

## Take away
:::takeaway
In your next planning conversation, before you turn to the form, ask the person and their family what a good life means to them, and write it down in their words.
:::
